procedural_history.originating_court: First Court of Munsiff at Serampur
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated May 11, 1966 of the Calcutta High Court in Criminal Revision No. 188 of 1966.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Magistrate convicted the respondents under s. 441/447 I.P.C., and the conviction was affirmed by the Sessions Judge. But the High Court, on a revision, acquitted the respondents as it was of the view that the appellant was not in actual possession of the property and that the complainant must not only be in actual possession but also be present at the time of the trespass so as to bring the offence under s. 441/447 I.P.C.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed by special leave against the High Court's judgment. The Supreme Court held that the High Court was in error and restored the judgment and order of the Magistrate.

directions: The judgment of the High Court is set aside.
The judgment and order of the Magistrate 1st Class Serampur, which was affirmed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Hoogly, is restored.

issue.issue_text: Whether a person who has obtained possession of a vacant piece of land through a court decree can be considered to be in 'actual possession' for the purposes of criminal trespass.

facts: The appellant filed a suit and, after 12 years of litigation, obtained a court decree for a piece of land.
In February 1963, the appellant was given "actual physical possession" of the land by a court official (Nazir) with police assistance, evicting the respondents.
For the next two weeks, the land remained vacant.
The respondents then trespassed onto this vacant land.
law: The Supreme Court established that for a vacant piece of land, the person who has legally obtained possession through a court order is considered to be in "actual possession."
The law does not require a person to be physically present on their vacant property at all times to be considered in "actual possession."
application: The High Court had ruled that the appellant was not in "actual possession" because the land was vacant and the appellant was not present at the time of the trespass.
The Supreme Court rejected this reasoning, stating that the High Court was in error.
The Supreme Court reasoned that since the land was lying vacant *after* the appellant had legally obtained possession, the "actual possession" must belong to the appellant.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that a person who has obtained possession of a vacant piece of land through a court decree is considered to be in 'actual possession' for the purposes of criminal trespass, even if they are not physically present on the land when the trespass occurs.

issue.issue_text: Whether the offence of criminal trespass under Section 441 IPC requires the person in possession of the property to be physically present at the time of the trespass to establish an 'intent to annoy'.

facts: The appellant filed a suit in 1951 and, after 12 years of litigation, obtained actual physical possession of a piece of land in February 1963, evicting the respondents with police assistance.
The land was left vacant by the appellant.
Two weeks after being evicted, the respondents trespassed onto the land and were found making preparations to construct bamboo structures.
The Magistrate and Sessions Judge convicted the respondents of criminal trespass under Sections 441/447 IPC.

The High Court acquitted the respondents, reasoning that the appellant was not in actual possession and, crucially, was not physically present at the time of the trespass, which it deemed necessary to establish an 'intent to annoy'.
law: The Supreme Court held that the law does not require the person in possession of the property, who is intended to be annoyed, to be physically present at the time of the trespass.
To establish the offence of criminal trespass, the court must be satisfied that the 'dominant intention' or 'aim' of the entry was to cause annoyance, intimidation, or insult.
application: The Court first corrected the High Court's factual finding, stating that the appellant was indeed in actual possession of the land, even though it was vacant.

The Court then directly addressed the legal issue, stating that the High Court was in error to require the complainant's physical presence. It explicitly held that "the law does not require that the intention must be to annoy a person who is actually present at the time of the trespass."

The Court analyzed the respondents' intent based on the circumstances. Given the long history of litigation and their recent forceful eviction, the Court concluded that the respondents could have had no realistic hope of retaining possession of the land.
Therefore, the Court found that the only 'dominant intention' that could have prompted the trespass so soon after the eviction was to annoy the appellant who had legally dispossessed them.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's position, holding that for the offence of criminal trespass under Section 441 IPC, the physical presence of the person in possession is not a legal requirement to prove that the trespasser had an 'intent to annoy'.

issue.issue_text: Whether the respondents' entry onto the land, shortly after being evicted following a lengthy legal battle, was done with the primary aim of annoying the appellant, thereby satisfying the 'intent' requirement for criminal trespass.

facts: The appellant and respondents were involved in a legal battle over the land for twelve years, starting in 1951.
The appellant won the lawsuit and, with police assistance, obtained actual physical possession of the land on February 3, 1963, evicting the respondents.
Just two weeks later, on February 17, 1963, the respondents trespassed back onto the land and began preparations to construct bamboo structures.
law: To establish criminal trespass, the prosecution must prove that the 'intent' to annoy, intimidate, or insult was the primary 'aim' or 'dominant intention' of the entry.
It is not sufficient to merely show that annoyance was a likely or natural consequence of the entry, even if the trespasser knew it would be.
The court must consider all relevant circumstances to determine what the dominant intention was.
application: The Court analyzed the circumstances to infer the respondents' dominant intention.
It reasoned that after a twelve-year legal battle and a recent, forceful eviction, the respondents could have had 'no hope' of successfully retaking and staying in possession of the land.

Because there was no other plausible or 'dominant intention' for their trespass (such as a genuine belief they could reclaim the property), the Court concluded that their only purpose must have been to annoy the appellant who had just legally secured possession.
The Court found the timing of the trespass—so soon after the eviction—to be a key indicator of their intent to annoy.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that on the facts of the case, there could be no doubt that the respondents' dominant intention in trespassing was to annoy the appellant. This satisfied the 'intent' requirement for the offence of criminal trespass.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a person who has obtained possession of a vacant piece of land through a court decree can be considered to be in 'actual possession' for the purposes of criminal trespass.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that he was in 'actual possession' of the land. He had obtained 'actual physical possession' through a court-ordered eviction with police help on February 3, 1963, and the land remained in his possession until the trespass occurred.
The fact that the land was lying vacant does not negate his possession; as the rightful possessor confirmed by a court decree, the actual possession must be considered his.
respondent_arguments: The respondents argued that the appellant was not in 'actual possession' of the property, a view that was accepted by the High Court. This implies they contended that since the land was vacant and the appellant was not physically present, he did not meet the standard of 'actual possession'.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the offence of criminal trespass under Section 441 IPC requires the person in possession of the property to be physically present at the time of the trespass to establish an 'intent to annoy'.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's position was that the law does not require the complainant to be physically present at the time of the trespass for the offence to be established. The intent to annoy can be inferred from the circumstances, regardless of the complainant's presence.
respondent_arguments: The respondents successfully argued in the High Court that the complainant must not only be in actual possession but also be physically present at the time of the trespass to establish an 'intent to annoy' under Section 441 IPC.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the respondents' entry onto the land, shortly after being evicted following a lengthy legal battle, was done with the primary aim of annoying the appellant, thereby satisfying the 'intent' requirement for criminal trespass.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the respondents' sole intention was to annoy him. This was evident from the history of the dispute, which began in 1951, and the fact that the respondents trespassed and began construction just two weeks after being forcibly evicted.

Given the lengthy and definitive legal battle that the respondents had lost, they could have had no realistic hope of retaining possession, meaning their dominant intention in re-entering the property must have been to annoy the appellant.
respondent_arguments: The respondents would have argued that their primary intent was not to annoy the appellant. While not explicitly stated in the text, their defense would have been that the prosecution failed to prove that annoyance was their dominant intention, as required by law.

cases.case_name: Mathuri and Others v. State of Punjab
cases.principle: To establish that an entry on property was with the intent to annoy, intimidate, or insult, it is necessary for the Court to be satisfied that causing such annoyance, intimidation, or insult was the aim of the entry. It is not sufficient to merely show that this was a likely consequence of the entry, even if known to the person entering.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: To establish the offense of criminal trespass, it must be proven that the primary aim of the entry was to annoy, intimidate, or insult the person in possession. It is insufficient to merely show that annoyance was a known or likely consequence of the entry. Furthermore, the law does not require the person in possession to be physically present at the time of the trespass, and a person who has lawfully obtained possession of vacant land is considered to be in actual possession of it.
obiter: The Magistrate was rather lenient to the respondent Fagu Shaw who seems to be an inveterate trespasser, and in the circumstances of this case the Magistrate should have sentenced him to imprisonment however short.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: On the specific facts of this case, where the respondents re-entered and began construction on a piece of land just two weeks after being forcibly evicted following a twelve-year legal battle, the court found it impossible to identify any dominant intention for the trespass other than to annoy the appellant. The respondents could have had no realistic hope of retaining possession, so their primary aim must have been to annoy the person who had just legally dispossessed them.
legal_tests_applied: To establish criminal trespass, the court must be satisfied that causing annoyance, intimidation, or insult was the 'aim of the entry'. It is not sufficient to merely show that annoyance was a natural consequence of the entry. In deciding the aim, the court must consider all relevant circumstances, including the probability of something other than causing annoyance being the dominant intention which prompted the entry. (Citing Mathuri and Others v. State of Punjab).
why_respondent_won: The High Court erred in its understanding of 'actual possession'; because the appellant had obtained possession through a court order and the land was lying vacant, the actual possession must be considered his.

The High Court was wrong in law to require the complainant's physical presence at the time of the trespass. The law does not require that the intention must be to annoy a person who is actually present at the time of the trespass.

Applying the correct legal test to the facts, the respondents' intent was clearly to annoy the appellant. The court reasoned: 'There could have been no hope on the part of the respondents that they would be able to stay in possession of the land... After twelve years of litiaation the appellant was able to obtain poss~sion, and only after two weells after that day the respondents chose to trespass and start construction.'
The court could not find 'any other dominant intention which prompted the trespass' besides the intent to annoy the appellant.
policy_considerations: The court's reasoning implicitly upholds the finality and authority of judicial orders. By finding criminal intent in a trespass that occurred so soon after a court-enforced eviction, it discourages parties from flouting the results of lengthy litigation.

There is a consideration for deterring repeat offenders, as the court noted that the Magistrate was 'rather lenient' with one respondent, describing him as an 'inveterate trespasser' who should have been sentenced to imprisonment.
